final_proof:
Let \(\theta=2\pi/n\), and use the standard convention \(\mathbb N_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\). Put \(v_k=e^{ik\theta}\) for \(0\le k<n\).

These points are distinct: if \(v_j=v_k\), then \(e^{i(j-k)\theta}=1\), so \((j-k)/n\) is an integer. Since \(|j-k|<n\), this forces \(j=k\). Thus \(U_n\) consists of exactly the \(n\) points \(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\).

Every one of these points lies on the unit circle centered at the origin, because \( |v_k|=|e^{ik\theta}|=1 \). Their arguments \(0,\theta,2\theta,\ldots,(n-1)\theta\) occur in strictly increasing order around that circle, and each successive pair, including \(v_{n-1},v_0\), subtends at the origin the same angle \(\theta=2\pi/n\). Join successive points in this cyclic order. This gives an \(n\)-sided polygon \(P\): the vertices are distinct, and the successive chords do not cross, since each lies in the sector bounded by the two corresponding successive radii (equivalently, these cyclically ordered points form an inscribed convex polygon).

The rotation \(R(w)=e^{i\theta}w\) maps \(v_k\) to \(v_{k+1}\), with indices read modulo \(n\), and hence maps every side of \(P\) to the next side and every interior angle to the next interior angle. Rotations preserve lengths and angles. Consequently all sides of \(P\) have the same length and all its interior angles have the same measure. Indeed, each side has length
\[|v_{k+1}-v_k|=|e^{i\theta}-1|=2\sin(\pi/n).\]
Therefore \(P\) is a regular \(n\)-sided polygon.

The unit circle centered at \((0,0)\) passes through every vertex of \(P\), so it circumscribes \(P\). Finally, \(v_0=e^0=1\), whose point in the complex plane is \((1,0)\), proving both stated properties.

For completeness, the initially specified number \(z\) is indeed one of these vertices. From \(z^n=1\) we have \(z\ne0\); writing \(z=re^{i\phi}\) gives \(r^n=1\), hence \(r=1\), and \(e^{in\phi}=1\), hence \(n\phi=2\pi m\) for some integer \(m\). Reducing \(m\) modulo \(n\) yields \(z=e^{2\pi i k/n}=v_k\) for a unique \(k\in\mathbb N_n\).
